note: EXAMPLE of the grouping ledger. Three routes, compared on the same five fields, with an explicit trade-off per group.

groups.label: Pretraining objectives on a whole unlabelled pool
groups.dimension: what is predicted during pretraining, and how much of the pool is touched

works.method_route: node-level plus graph-level masked/contrastive objectives, combined in one schedule
works.data_setting: one fixed unlabelled molecular corpus, used whole
works.evaluation: downstream classification and regression with a linear or fine-tuned head
works.conclusion: objective choice matters more than encoder capacity, and naive pretraining can hurt
works.limitation: corpus treated as a single pool; pretraining cost is not modelled

works.method_route: contrastive learning with atom masking, bond deletion and subgraph positives
works.data_setting: full unlabelled pool, every molecule scanned each epoch
works.evaluation: MoleculeNet property benchmarks against supervised baselines
works.conclusion: contrastive positives built from chemical subgraphs beat supervised training in low label regimes
works.limitation: number of forward passes grows with pool size and dominates the compute budget

works.method_route: mutual-information maximisation between graph and substructure embeddings
works.data_setting: any unlabelled graph set; choice of set does not enter the objective
works.conclusion: unsupervised objectives are competitive with supervised pretraining on graph-level tasks
works.limitation: objective is agnostic to which graphs are used, so redundant graphs cost compute without changing the objective

works.method_route: graph transformer with node- and edge-level self-supervision
works.conclusion: large-scale transformer pretraining transfers to molecular tasks
works.limitation: no experiment asks whether a smaller corpus would suffice

comparison.tradeoff: All four routes spend their effort on the objective and none on which molecules are used: contrastive or generative objectives differ in sample efficiency per epoch, whereas GPU time per epoch is set by the pool size they all take as given. R0003 shows objective choice is decisive, which makes the corpus question invisible rather than answered.
comparison.best_for: tasks where the unlabelled pool is small enough that scanning it repeatedly is affordable

groups.label: Selecting a subset of the unlabelled pool
groups.dimension: what signal drives selection, and what it optimises

works.method_route: k-centre greedy selection in a fixed embedding
works.evaluation: error of a model trained on the subset, bounded relative to the full set
works.conclusion: a bounded k-centre subset reproduces full-set error
works.limitation: the guarantee is stated for a fixed feature space and does not transfer to learned representations

works.method_route: per-molecule informativeness estimated for the downstream label budget
works.data_setting: unlabelled molecular pool with a 100-label downstream task
works.conclusion: label-aware selection gains up to 8.6% over random pretraining
works.limitation: selection is guided by label scarcity alone and ignores the cost of the pretraining corpus itself

works.method_route: empirical scaling law of downstream error against corpus size
works.data_setting: a fixed, uncurated corpus across three model families and eighteen tasks
works.conclusion: returns flatten past roughly one million molecules
works.limitation: the law is fitted on an uncurated corpus, so it cannot say whether a curated subset reaches the same plateau

comparison.dimension: selection signal vs what it optimises
comparison.tradeoff: R0007 optimises coverage of a feature space that does not yet exist, R0009 optimises for the label budget but treats the corpus as free, and R0010 shows the corpus size matters yet assumes it is uncurated. None of the three optimises the cost of pretraining itself, which is the quantity that decides whether low-resource pretraining is affordable.
comparison.best_for: settings where pretraining compute is abundant and only labels are scarce

groups.label: Encoders and geometric priors
groups.dimension: what inductive bias the encoder supplies, and whether it is pretrained at all

works.method_route: first-order approximation of a localized spectral filter
works.data_setting: citation and knowledge graphs; node-level tasks
works.conclusion: localized propagation scales linearly in edges
works.limitation: one hop per layer, so global spectral information needs many layers

works.method_route: message passing over a fixed neighbourhood radius, unified framework
works.conclusion: message passing reaches state of the art on QM9
works.limitation: a fixed radius means a single step cannot see beyond it

works.method_route: continuous-filter convolution giving rotation and translation invariance
works.evaluation: mean absolute error on molecular targets
works.conclusion: physically motivated filters reach state of the art without pretraining
works.limitation: trained from scratch per task, so every dataset pays the full training cost

comparison.dimension: inductive bias vs dependence on labelled data
comparison.tradeoff: These encoders bake in the geometry and topology of molecules, and R0008 shows that is enough to reach state of the art on a single task; the price is that each new task retrains from scratch. The bias and the pretraining question are therefore separable: the encoder fixes what can be represented, and selection fixes what is learned from.
comparison.best_for: single-task settings with enough labelled data to train from scratch
